column2: All the urgent times for acts, best of the Bharatas, are fixed; so you should stand adorned at the right time, a great protector; this turn of acts goes on always like a wheel.
You should always strive justly to build up the treasury, great king, and avoid the opposite of both kinds.
All the country people, Pandava, and the town's leaders, assembly-members and traders should do your work.
You should always observe, Yudhishthira, the weak points of your own and of others, among your own and among enemies.
Men in other lands who are valiant in all works should be favoured by you with fitting allowances for their good.
You should show regard to the learned who seek merit, king, and you should be unshakable like the great mountain Meru.
Among all four kinds of enemies and aggressors, you should know the friend, the enemy and the enemy's friend, scourge of foes.
So ministers, countryside, strongholds, hard places and forces, best of the Kurus, are theirs as they wish.
And those twelve of kings, Kaunteya, of varied kinds, and sixty-twelve qualities with ministers chief, lord,
teachers who know policy call these the circle; on it the six-fold policy depends, Yudhishthira; learn it.
Increase and decay and the stationary should be known, delight of the Kurus; by seventy-two, mighty-armed one, then those who practise the six-fold policy.
When your own side is strong and the enemy's weak, Kaunteya, a king should march, having fought his enemies; when his own side is weak, he should take refuge in peace.
A great store of goods should also be made, O Bharata, when one is able to march quickly.
Then everything should be arranged and the station not divided; land of little fruit should be given to the opposite one, O Bharata.
Gold and base metal in plenty, an ally weak and without treasury: skilled in peace-making, he should not himself accept the opposite.
For the sake of peace you should seek a prince, best of the Bharatas; but a hostile one is not to be given, son, in any danger; and you, knowing counsel, should strive by a means for his release.
A king should consider the constituents of the kingdom and the like in order, and the strength and weakness of calamities in pairs.
Oppression, paralysis and breaking the treasury of enemies are to be done carefully by one guarding his own realm.
One who has come for refuge, a neighbouring chieftain, is not to be harmed by one desiring growth; Kaunteya, one desiring to conquer the earth should not harm him.
You should use the way of breaking up confederacies with your ministers, by good gathering and restraint of the wicked.
And the weak should always not be relied on against the strong; you should stand like a reed, tiger among kings.
If a strong king attacks a weak one so, he should by degrees turn him back by conciliation and other means.
Unable to fight, he should go forth with his ministers, with the treasury, the townspeople, the army and others who do his good.
If it is not possible for all, he should go forth with the chief of them in order; thus liberation may be gained, and even the body alone.
King of kings, you should besiege, having cut his two-sidedness, and remember that the enemy is satisfied, nourished, strong and self-possessed.
At the time of besieging the opposite is done; at the time of crushing, king of kings, retreat is then better.
One should then bring about calamity and breaking of the enemies, weakening and terrifying, and in war great destruction.
A king about to march, skilled in the scriptures, should consider threefold the strength of himself and of the enemy.
A man endowed with the power of enterprise, of lordship and of counsel, O Bharata, should march; otherwise not.
A king should take the hereditary force, the allied force, the forest force, the hired force and the guild force.
Of these, king, the allied force is not better than the hereditary, and I think the guild force and hired force are alike.
So the force of spies is equal to each, king; it is to be known in the times of forces when the king's time has come.
Many are the alternatives of calamities, Pandava; a king should always allay them by conciliation and the like.
A king should march with six forces, joined with place and time, with forces and with his own qualities, scourge of foes.
A king, satisfied, nourished in strength and fond of growth, should march; and when summoned, a king should march even in unfavourable seasons.
Where a river has posts and stones, chiefly horses and chariots, its banks and shores covered with banner-trees, much mud from foot soldiers and elephants, a king should march to destroy his rival.
Then by contrivance, Bharata, the cart-array, the lotus-array and the thunderbolt-array: Ushanas knew that science, and it is ordained there, lord.
Having pressed down the enemy's force and gladdened his own force, he should join battle on his own ground and likewise on the enemy's.
A king should quiet what is gained, place wealthy men there, and, knowing his own land, deal with it by conciliation and the rest.
So too, great king, one should sustain the body here, and after death what is to be done is the supreme good of oneself.
Doing so, the king hears good words in this world, and after death gains heaven, protecting his subjects by dharma.
You should behave so, best of the Kurus, for your subjects' good, always for the gaining of both worlds, dear one.
You were told this before by Bhishma, Krishna and Vidura; and I too must tell you with love, best of kings.
Do all this justly, giver of rich fees; dear to your subjects, you will gain happiness in heaven.
A king who sacrifices with a thousand horse sacrifices, or one who protects his subjects by dharma, gains equal fruit.
With Bhishma gone to heaven, Madhusudana gone, Vidura and Sanjaya, who else is fit to speak to me?
What you now instruct me, standing in my good, I shall do, king; be at ease, Bharata.
[Vaishampayana] Thus addressed by the wise king of dharma, the royal sage wished to give leave to Kunti's son, bull of the Bharatas.
Son, rest awhile; my fatigue too is great. Having said this, the king then entered Gandhari's house.
As he sat on a seat, the goddess Gandhari, who practised dharma and knew time, said at the right time to her husband, like Prajapati:
Permitted by the great sage Vyasa himself, with Yudhishthira's consent, when will you go to the forest?
[Dhritarashtra] "Gandhari, I am permitted by my great-souled father himself; with Yudhishthira's consent I shall go to the forest before long.
I wish to give wealth for all those sons who played the evil dice, wealth that follows them in feeling after death, having assembled all the constituents of the kingdom in my house."
Then to the brahmins and kings gathered from various lands the greatly radiant king Dhritarashtra said:

Hear, with one-pointed mind, brahmins, people of Kuru-Jangala, kshatriyas, vaishyas and shudras assembled.
mahabharata:15:13.14	You Kurus have long lived together with me, friends of one another, devoted to one another's good.
mahabharata:15:13.15	What I say now when this time has come, you should do, without hesitation at my word.
mahabharata:15:13.16	My mind is set on going to the forest with Gandhari, with the consent of Vyasa and of Kunti's son the king; you too should give leave; let there be no doubt about this.
mahabharata:15:13.17	This love between us and you is eternal, and I think kings have it in no other lands.
mahabharata:15:13.18	I am tired with age and bereft of sons, and thin with fasting, blameless ones, along with Gandhari.
mahabharata:15:13.19	With the kingdom gone to Yudhishthira I have gained great happiness; I think it better than Duryodhana's lordship, good ones.
mahabharata:15:13.20	What other course is there for me, blind, aged, with sons slain, except the forest, greatly fortunate ones? You should give me leave.
Hearing his words, all those people of Kuru-Jangala wept, O bull of the Bharatas, in voices choked with tears.
As they said nothing, given up to sorrow and grief, the greatly radiant Dhritarashtra again said this:

And as my brother Pandu was dear to you, he too protected you rightly, and you know that.
mahabharata:15:14.3	Whatever service I did to you well or ill, blameless ones, that should be forgiven by you, tireless ones.
mahabharata:15:14.4	And that Duryodhana enjoyed this kingdom without thorn: even then that fool, ill-minded, did not offend you.
mahabharata:15:14.5	By that ill-minded one's offence, out of pride of kings, there was a great crush, then through the wrong done by me.
mahabharata:15:14.6	Whether that was well or ill done by me, you should not keep it in your hearts; you should give me leave.
mahabharata:15:14.7	Give leave, thinking: this one is aged, his sons slain, grieved, and is the son of former kings.
mahabharata:15:14.8	And this pitiable, aged ascetic Gandhari, afflicted with grief for her sons, begs you along with me.
mahabharata:15:14.9	Knowing these two aged ones with sons slain and grieved, give leave; good fortune to you; we go, and you are our refuge.
He has four brothers as counsellors, of vast radiance, like guardians of the world, all seeing dharma and wealth.
This Yudhishthira, greatly radiant, like the blessed Brahma, lord of all beings and the world, will protect you.
Thinking that it must be said, I tell you: this trust has been given by me; Yudhishthira is for all of you, and you have been made a trust for that hero by me.
If any wrong has been done by my sons, or by another of mine, you should forgive it.
I have never before felt anger toward you, who are exceedingly devoted to your elders; this is my salutation with folded hands.
For those of unsteady minds, greedy and wilful, I beg all of you, blameless ones, along with Gandhari."
So addressed by the king, the townspeople and country folk, their eyes full of tears, said nothing and looked at one another.
When they fell silent, their throats choked with tears, King Dhritarashtra spoke again to them.

Me, aged and with sons slain, lamenting in many ways with this wife of dharma, pitiable, good ones,
mahabharata:15:15.4	permitted by my father himself, Krishna Dvaipayana, and by the king who knows dharma, for forest dwelling, knowers of dharma:
mahabharata:15:15.5	I beg you again and again, bowed with my head, blameless ones; you should give me leave with Gandhari.
Hearing the king of the Kurus' piteous words, all the people of Kuru-Jangala gathered there wept, O king.
Covering their faces with their upper garments and hands, they wept for a moment, afflicted with grief, as for father and mother.
With hearts become empty, bearing the grief of Dhritarashtra's departure, they seemed to lose their senses.
Having subdued that distress born of parting from the Kuru king, they slowly said their opinions to one another.
Then the aged Samba, honoured, skilled in matters, a Rigvedic brahmin, began to speak, O king.
Having honoured the great king and addressed that assembly, the bold, wise brahmin said to the king:

King, all the speech of these people is entrusted to me; I shall tell it, hero; hear it, lord of men.
mahabharata:15:15.14	As you say, king of kings, all this is so, lord; there is no falsehood in it; you are our friend and we are yours.
mahabharata:15:15.15	Never has any king of this line been one who, protecting subjects, was unkind to his subjects.
mahabharata:15:15.16	You protect us like fathers and brothers; and Duryodhana did nothing improper, king.
mahabharata:15:15.17	As the knower of dharma, the sage, Satyavati's son, says, so do, great king, for he is our supreme teacher.
mahabharata:15:15.18	Abandoned by you, given to sorrow and grief, we shall be long, king, carried off by your hundreds of virtues.
mahabharata:15:15.19	As we were guarded by Shantanu and King Chitrangada, embraced by Bhishma's valour, by your father, king of the earth,
mahabharata:15:15.20	and by Pandu, king, who was joined to your counsel, so too we were well protected by King Duryodhana.
mahabharata:15:15.21	Your son did us not even the slightest wrong, king; we were as trusting in that king as in a father, as you know well.
mahabharata:15:15.22	So for a thousand years we shall find happiness, king, protected by the wise, steadfast son of Kunti.
mahabharata:15:15.23	Of the ancient royal sages, upholders of your line, Kuru, Samvarana and the rest, and the wise Bharata,
mahabharata:15:15.24	this righteous one of rich fees follows the conduct; there is nothing to be said here, great king, not even a very slight thing.
mahabharata:15:15.25	We have lived happily, always protected by you; there is not even a slight wrong in you with your son.
mahabharata:15:15.26	As to what you say regarding Duryodhana in this crush of kinsmen, there too I shall appease you, delight of the Kurus.

We know it as fate, which cannot be resisted; fate cannot be overcome by human effort.
mahabharata:15:16.3	Eighteen akshauhinis, great king, assembled and were slain in eighteen days, with ten leading warriors,
mahabharata:15:16.4	Bhishma, Drona, Kripa and others, the great-souled Karna, the hero Yuyudhana, Dhrishtadyumna,
mahabharata:15:16.5	and the four sons of Pandu, Bhima, Arjuna and the twins, king; this destruction of people was done by those made by the power of fate.
mahabharata:15:16.6	In battle, a kshatriya especially must meet death by the weapon in the world, as a kshatriya.
mahabharata:15:16.7	By those tigers among men, endowed with knowledge and strength of arm, the whole earth with its horses, chariots and elephants was struck down.
mahabharata:15:16.8	That king, your great-minded son, does not offend; neither do you, nor your servants, nor Karna, nor the Saubala.
mahabharata:15:16.9	That the best of the Kurus and thousands of kings perished was all done by fate; who can say anything about it here?

These subjects will follow, in smooth and rough, the Pandavas, best of the Kuru line, adorned by good conduct.
mahabharata:15:16.15	The Pandava protects the brahmin gifts, the grants and the exemptions, and the gifts of former kings.
mahabharata:15:16.16	Far-sighted, of resolved mind, always like Vaishravana, with ministers not mean, this great-minded son of Kunti,
mahabharata:15:16.17	compassionate even to enemies, pure, best of the Bharatas, uprightly seeing, wise, always protects us like sons.
mahabharata:15:16.18	Through association with the people they will not do anything displeasing to the son of Dharma, royal sage, and so Bhima, Arjuna and the others.
mahabharata:15:16.19	Dull to the gentle, like venomous snakes to the harsh, the great-souled Kauravas are valiant and devoted to the townspeople's good.
mahabharata:15:16.20	Neither Kunti, nor Panchali, nor Ulupi, nor the Satvati will ever do anything adverse to these people.
mahabharata:15:16.21	This affection made and increased by you, Yudhishthira, the townspeople and country folk will not turn their backs on.
mahabharata:15:16.22	The great chariot-fighter sons of Kunti, though men may be unrighteous, will protect them, devoted to dharma.
mahabharata:15:16.23	So, king, having put away mental pain from Yudhishthira, do the tasks of dharma; salutations to you, best of the Bharatas.
[Vaishampayana] That dharmic, consequence-rich word of his was accepted by all the people as "Well done, well done."
And Dhritarashtra, honouring that speech again and again, slowly dismissed all the subjects then.
Honoured by them and looked on with good will, the king, with folded hands, honoured the people, best of the Bharatas.
Then the king entered his house with Gandhari; learn what he did when the night had passed.
Going on the king's word, the greatly radiant best of the wise said to Yudhishthira, the lord, the unfailing:

Dhritarashtra, great king, consecrated for forest life, will go to the forest, king, when this Kartika has come.
mahabharata:15:17.4	He wishes something from you, best of the Kurus: he wishes to give a shraddha for the great-souled son of Ganga,
mahabharata:15:17.5	for Drona, Somadatta and the wise Bahlika, and all his sons and friends who were slain, and if you permit, for the Saindhava, the vile.
Hearing Vidura's words, Yudhishthira was glad, and the Pandava Gudakesha honoured him.
But Bhima of firm anger did not accept Vidura's word then, remembering what Duryodhana had done.
Knowing Bhimasena's intent, Phalguna Kirithin bowed a little and said to Bhima:

Bhima, the king, our aged father consecrated for forest life, wishes to give funeral offerings for all his friends.
mahabharata:15:17.11	By good fortune, mighty-armed one, Dhritarashtra begs today, who was formerly begged by us; see the turn of time.
mahabharata:15:17.12	He who was lord of the whole earth, king, with his offspring slain by enemies, wishes to go to the forest.
mahabharata:15:17.13	Let there be no other thought in you, tiger among men; let the sight be from giving; anything else would be disgraceful and unrighteous, mighty-armed one.
mahabharata:15:17.14	Serve the king, your elder brother, the lord; you are fit to give and not to withhold, best of the Bharatas. And the king of dharma honoured Kunti's son who spoke so.
But Bhimasena, angry, said then: "Phalguna, we shall perform here Bhishma's funeral rites,
and those of King Somadatta, Bhurishravas, the royal sage Bahlika and the great-souled Drona.
Kunti will give shraddhas for Karna and the other friends, tiger among men; the Kaurava king must not.
So my mind runs; let not our enemies rejoice; let Duryodhana and all the rest go from pain to greater pain, by whom this whole earth was slain, those disgraces of the family.
How can you forget, today, the enmity of twelve years, the going into hiding that increased Draupadi's grief? Where was Dhritarashtra's love for us then?
Clad in black deer-skin, stripped of ornaments, you went with the daughter of Panchala to the king; where were Drona and Bhishma then, and Somadatta?
When you lived thirteen years in the forest on wild fare, your father, the elder, did not look on you as a father.
Have you forgotten, Partha, that this disgrace of the family, of bad conduct, said to Vidura at the dice, 'What have you won?'"
To him speaking so, King Yudhishthira, Kunti's son, said to his wise brother, rebuking him, "Be quiet."
The good, best of men, do not remember offences but remember good deeds, and do not break the bounds of purpose.
On my word, Kshatta, tell this to the Kaurava king: as much as he wishes to give for his sons, I give.
And for Bhishma and all the other friends who did good: from my treasury, lord; let Bhima not be ill-minded.
[Vaishampayana] Thus addressed, the king of dharma praised Arjuna, and Bhimasena looked sideways at Dhananjaya.
Then the wise Yudhishthira said to Vidura: "The king should not be angry with Bhimasena.
Bhima was tormented by snow, rain and heat and by many sorrows in the forest, as you know, wise one.
But on my word tell the best of the Bharatas the king: whatever you wish and as much as you wish, take from my house.
The king should be told: 'Do not take to heart the spite that Bhima, greatly grieved, does.'"
[Vidura] "Yudhishthira the king has been told your words first, and the greatly radiant one, hearing your words, praised them.
And the greatly radiant Bibhatsu offers you his houses, the wealth in his house, and even his own life.
And your son the king of dharma, royal sage, gives permission for the kingdom, lives, wealth, and whatever else there is.
But Bhima, remembering many sorrows, as if with difficulty, the mighty-armed one, sighing, agreed.
He, urged by the king of righteous conduct and by his brother Bibhatsu, mighty-armed, was set again in friendship.
The king of dharma said to you, 'Do not be angry', and Bhima, remembering that enmity, would act unjustly.
So, king, this dharma of kshatriyas mostly so, and this Vrikodara is devoted to battle and to kshatriya dharma.
For Vrikodara's sake, I and Arjuna again and again appease you, king, since you are the lord here.
So the king and the Pandavas, and Dhananjaya, told me; what is to be done next, you should tell."
Thus addressed by Vidura, Dhritarashtra welcomed it and set his mind on a great gift on Kartika, Janamejaya.
Then he saw thousands of suitable brahmins, best of sages, for Bhishma and for his friends' sons,
had food and drink, vehicles and garments prepared, gold, jewels, women and men servants and furnishings,
blankets, deer-skins, jewels, villages, fields, goats and sheep, ornaments, elephants, horses, maidens and fair women; assigning to each, that best of kings gave to brahmins.
Naming Drona, Bhishma, Somadatta and Bahlika, King Duryodhana and his sons, each separately, and Jayadratha and his friends everywhere,
that shraddha sacrifice grew, with fees of many cows and wealth, and floods of much wealth and jewels, then with Yudhishthira's consent.
Men, accountants and scribes constantly asked the king there, by Yudhishthira's word:
Command: what is to be given to these? Let it be given; and so what was asked was seen present at the end of each word.
Where a hundred was to be given, a thousand was given, and where a thousand, ten thousand, by the word of the wise king, Kunti's son.
So, great king, he gave funeral gifts for his sons and grandsons, for the ancestors, for himself and for Gandhari.
When he was tired, he gave many gifts; then the upholder of the Kurus completed the gift sacrifice.
So that Kaurava king made a festival of giving, rich in actors, dancers and singers, with many foods, drinks and fees.
Having given gifts so for ten days, Ambika's son, bull of the Bharatas, became free of debt to his sons and grandsons.
The wise one with Gandhari, having rejoiced by rule and had a sacrifice performed by Veda-master brahmins on Kartika,
putting the Agnihotra first, wearing bark and deer-skin, the king, surrounded by his daughters-in-law, then went out of the house.
Then the Kuru women and the Pandavas' women, and the other women of the Kaurava royal line, a cry arose from them as the king, Vichitravirya's son, set out.
Then the king, honouring that house with parched grain and varied flowers and rewarding all his servants with wealth, left and went on, lord of men.
Then King Yudhishthira, with folded hands, trembling, his throat choked with tears, lamented loudly, "Alas, great king, good one, where will you go?" and fell on the ground, dear one.
Arjuna, tormented by sharp grief, sighing again and again, said "Not so" to Yudhishthira, and restrained him and lifted him up, sinking.
Vrikodara and Phalguna the heroes, Madri's two sons, Vidura and Sanjaya, the vaishya woman's son with Gautama, Dhaumya and the brahmins followed, their throats choked with tears.
Kunti, bearing on her shoulder the hand of Gandhari, whose eyes were bound as she walked, and the king, laying his hand on Gandhari's shoulder, went forth, assured.
The cry of those weeping women then was loud from grief, king, like osprey females; then the women of brahmins, kshatriyas, vaishyas and shudras poured out on all sides.
At his departure the townspeople in Gajahvaya grew very sorrowful, king, as when the Pandavas went before, at the dice, in the Kauravas' hall.
Women who had never been seen by moon or sun, when the great forest was gone to by the Kaurava king, afflicted with grief came onto the royal road.
The wise king, trembling with folded hands, with difficulty went out by the royal road, crowded with men and women.
He went out of Gajasahvaya by the Vardhamana gate and again and again dismissed that flood of people.
Vidura, with the king's consent, was ready to go to the forest, and also Sanjaya the minister, son of Gavalgana, the charioteer.
Dhritarashtra, giving Kripa and the great chariot-fighter Yuyutsu into Yudhishthira's care, sent them back.
When the townspeople had turned back, the king, with his women, wished to turn back, permitted by Dhritarashtra.
Approaching his mother Kunti, bull of the Bharatas, he said, "I shall follow the king; you should turn back.
Surrounded by your daughters-in-law, queen, you should go to the city; let this righteous king go, resolved on austerity."
Thus addressed by the king of dharma, her eyes full of tears, Kunti, holding Gandhari, then said:

My heart is surely of iron, dull as I am, son, that it does not split into a hundred pieces as I do not see the sun's son.
mahabharata:15:22.13	What can I do in such a case, scourge of foes? This is my greatest fault, that the sun's son was not made known; for that, mighty-armed one, you should give the best gift.
mahabharata:15:22.14	Always, with your brothers, scourge of foes, you should remain dear to the elder brother and to Draupadi.
mahabharata:15:22.15	Bhimasena, Arjuna and Nakula, delight of the Kurus, you should keep composed, hero; the burden of the family has now come to you.
mahabharata:15:22.16	I shall live in the forest serving the feet of my father-in-law and mother-in-law, with Gandhari, an ascetic smeared with dirt.
In every way I shall take the Vrishni women, the children and the aged, and bring them to Indraprastha, scourge of foes.
By the all-knowing, knower of rules, knower of dharma, good one, beyond the senses, pure, whose soul is cultivated by austerity,
